city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.p_yest: The high of 44°F was typical for November 13. The normal high for the date is 49°F, and the record is 69°F (1964). The low of 27°F was typical for November 13.
text.t_rec: Record highs keep coming. Record lows have nearly stopped.
text.p_rec: If Concord's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Concord has set 20 standing record lows, far fewer than the 62 that chance alone would give, and 96 record highs, far more than the 62 that chance alone would give. The 2010s hold the most record highs of any decade (36). Concord's all-time high is 102°F, on July 4, 1911.
text.t_chg: Concord's nights have warmed since 1986. Its days have warmed.
text.p_chg: Across 157 complete years: Concord's average low shows no clear change: −0.02°F per decade, a range (−0.08 to +0.04) that includes zero. Concord's average high has risen +0.15°F per decade (95% range +0.10 to +0.20), about +2.3°F since 1869. The last 40 years tell a different story: since 1986, lows have risen +0.86°F per decade (95% range +0.52 to +1.19) and highs have risen +0.60°F per decade (95% range +0.26 to +0.94). The full record joins different observing sites over the years, and a move (for example, from the city to a cooler airport) can hide or exaggerate a long-run trend, so the recent decades are the clearer guide here.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in 1 of 12 months; 4 months fell. Highs rose in 7 of 12 months.

text.p_rain: Concord's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (+0.21 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 41.9 inches a year. The wettest year was 2008 (57.97 in); the driest, 1965 (24.17 in).
